name: The 20 MW threshold
desc: Apply the reforms to new loads over 20 MW; DOE asked whether that line is right, or needed at all.

letters.desc: Alliant Energy supports raising the applicability threshold from 20 MW to at least 100 MW. A 20 MW floor would pull in smaller, less impactful loads, creating backlogs and defeating the ANOPR's efficiency goals. A higher threshold focuses limited study resources on the largest, most grid-impactful projects.
quotes: Alliant Energy strongly recommends that the Commission increase the minimum applicability threshold from 20 MW to at least 100 MW.

Such a low threshold would unnecessarily draw numerous smaller, less impactful projects into the interconnection process, creating backlogs, congestion, and delays that undermine the very objectives of the ANOPR.

letters.desc: Amazon Energy proposes concrete readiness criteria for fast-track qualification and for deterring speculative requests, such as committed customers, secured permits, site control, secured financing or corporate commitments, and executed service or construction agreements.
quotes: Amazon Energy encourages the Commission to include in any rule a "fast track" or priority processing track for large load projects that can demonstrate a high degree of readiness (e.g., projects that have (i) committed customers, (ii) secured all necessary permits, (iii) site control, (iv) secured financing or corporate commitments, and/or (v) an executed service agreement).

requiring large load interconnection customers to make upfront study deposits, demonstrate a degree of project readiness (e.g., site control or an executed facilities construction contract), and face withdrawal penalties if they exit after certain milestones will discourage non-viable or speculative large load requests.

letters.desc: ACC argues interconnection studies should reflect actual load profiles and flexibility commitments rather than assuming peak draw at all times, ensuring cost allocations are fair and accurate.
quotes: ensure that cost responsibility reflects a load's real-world impact, including any curtailment commitments or co-located generation and storage

letters.desc: ATC recommends that any new requirements apply only to loads that fail specific operating criteria such as ramp rate or ride-through capability, limiting the rule to genuinely non-conforming loads.
quotes: requirements should be narrowly tailored to focus on experienced issues and allow maximum flexibility.
the Commission should consider adopting threshold applicability requirements based upon specific operating characteristics.

Limiting applicability to the subset of loads that do not meet with certain operating criteria could provide adequate controls, ensure reliability, contain costs, while preserving the flexibility for transmission owners such as ATC to continue to interconnect traditional, conforming loads based upon our existing interconnection processes.

letters.org: Americans for a Clean Energy Grid
letters.desc: ACEG recommends that large loads of 50 MW or more be required to make stringent financial commitments and be reported to regional transmission planners, so forecasts are reliable and not inflated by speculative requests. The filing notes that rolled-up forecasts from individual transmission owners distort regional planning and create delays.
quotes: in the final rule, load forecasting was treated as it has always been: through rolling up the forecasts from individual transmission owners within a region. While this may have worked for conventional increases in demand, this does not work for the large loads being forecasted today.

the Commission could do more—either through a supplemental rulemaking associated with Order No. 1920 or provision of guidance in this proceeding—to require transmission planners to independently assess load forecasts and determine that they are sufficiently robust and as accurate as possible.

a requirement that large loads (50 MW or larger, for instance) are backed by stringent financial commitments and are reported to regional transmission planners so that significant loads can be adequately supported and integrated into the larger grid.

letters.desc: Arevia advocates for a 99 MW threshold rather than 20 MW to account for the scale of modern AI data center loads.
quotes: Arevia believes that FERC should consider an even larger threshold of above 99 MW, due to the increasing size of Artificial Intelligence data center loads.

letters.desc: If FERC proceeds, the APSC recommends a minimum load threshold of no less than 100 MW to limit federal rule scope to genuinely large loads.
quotes: limits any final rule to transmission‑level engineering studies only; recognizes existing regional processes such as SPP's proposed HILLS and CHILLS as compliant alternatives; sets a minimum load threshold of no less than 100 MW; and requires robust coordination with state regulators.

letters.desc: CAISO endorses the 20 MW threshold as a clear, already-understood demarcation that mirrors the figure used for generation and storage facilities. CAISO warns that higher thresholds would invite developers to split facilities to avoid jurisdiction.
quotes: The 20 MW threshold has proven to be a reliable figure to assess the risk a generation or storage facility represents to the transmission grid.

much higher MW thresholds may incentivize developers to create multiple facilities each right under the limit to avoid jurisdiction, rather than a single facility that benefits the facility and the grid from economy of scale.

letters.desc: The CPUC shifts its position toward a higher MW threshold in response to Initial Comments showing broad variation across regions. It also supports defining the data center customer class by characteristics beyond MW alone, to protect local manufacturers and enable fair retail cost allocation.
quotes: the CPUC shifts its positions on the MW threshold towards a higher value and expands consideration of metrics for defining this large load customer class.

MW metrics alone may not be the defining feature of this type of load.  The CPUC agrees with the Ohio Office of Federal Energy Advocate ("Ohio FEA") that data centers are a unique customer class, and identifying them based on their exceptional characteristics is not unduly discriminatory.
if a final rule includes a nationwide MW threshold, the conservative next-best option is to set a threshold on the higher end of the spectrum of those proposed in Comments.

letters.desc: The Center supports the DOE's recommended 20 MW applicability threshold and is open to an even lower figure. Industry proposals of 100 to 200 MW would exclude many data centers and cryptomining operations, undermining the reform's scope.
quotes: The Center generally supports DOE's second Principle, which recommends that any regulatory reforms apply to 'new loads greater than 20 MW,' although even a lower threshold might be appropriate.
Setting a 100 MW threshold would therefore exclude a significant number of new electricity-intensive facilities seeking to connect to the grid.

letters.org: CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES
letters.desc: The Chamber recommends raising the minimum large load threshold from the proposed 20 MW to 75 or 100 MW so grid operators focus on truly impactful interconnections and queues are not overwhelmed by smaller loads.
quotes: the Chamber recommends that the floor for “large load” interconnections be raised to 75 or 100 MW. An increased minimum threshold would better reflect the scale of modern large load projects, ensuring that regulatory frameworks are aligned with current and future industry needs.

letters.desc: Constellation supports adopting standardized study deposits, readiness requirements, and withdrawal penalties for large loads, similar to Order No. 2003 for generators. Without clear filed standards, Transmission Owners retain discretion to delay or deny large load requests.
quotes: The lack of consistent standards for large loads and hybrid facilities creates a vacuum that leaves Transmission Owners with significant discretion to delay or deny large-load and co-location proposals and to impose terms that are neither just nor reasonable.

letters.desc: Critical Loop supports cost-causation principles as the threshold for determining large-load interconnection charges, and argues these principles should also reward loads that verifiably reduce system costs through LLFC commitments.
quotes: Large loads should pay the costs they cause, and they should receive appropriate treatment, including access to expedited, flexible interconnection pathways and transparent queue treatment, when they verifiably reduce needed system investments and help lower long-run costs for other ratepayers through LLFC-style commitments and bring-your-own-capacity arrangements.

letters.desc: Crusoe argues the proposed 20 MW threshold is too low and would flood the queue with smaller projects better handled through existing processes. It recommends a 100 MW floor so that streamlined federal rules target only the largest, highest-impact facilities like Crusoe's own 1,200 MW projects.
quotes: The proposed 20 MW threshold for the new large load and hybrid facility interconnections may be too low to efficiently advance AI deployment.  The Commission should consider raising the threshold to facilities above 100 MW.

streamlined processes should prioritize large facilities above 100 MW.  For example, Crusoe has under development facilities in the 1,200 MW range with both grid interconnection and onsite natural gas production.

letters.desc: EPSA asks the Commission to clarify that the 20 MW threshold applies to the full expected load, not just the initial phase, so that phased ramp-up projects are captured from the start.
quotes: it is important that the Commission clarify that the established threshold is based on the full expected load, even if a large load customer ramps up to that amount in phases.

letters.desc: ECA finds 20 MW a reasonable starting threshold for triggering large load interconnection requirements, viewing it as a practical tool to limit regulatory burden without undermining jurisdictional reach.
quotes: ECA believes that 20 MW is a reasonable starting place for defining the new loads that should be subject to new requirements to have large load interconnection procedures and agreements in place.

letters.desc: Eolian recommends FERC adopt a straightforward capacity and voltage threshold (such as 20 MW at 60 to 100 kV) to define which large loads are subject to federal interconnection rules. This replaces the ambiguous seven-factor test and eliminates litigation risk that would delay the rulemaking's benefits.
quotes: the Commission should establish a bright-line standard over which large loads are subject to a federally-regulated interconnection process instead of relying on the seven-factor test.

the Commission could establish that the interconnection of large loads (e.g., 20 MW, as proposed by the ANOPR) to facilities with voltage greater than or equal to between 60-100 kV would be subject to federal interconnection standards.

letters.desc: Eolian supports bright-line capacity and voltage thresholds over the seven-factor test, which it views as too slow and litigable to provide investment certainty. Based on its own project experience, Eolian recommends 75 to 100 MW as a capacity floor, combined with a voltage threshold above 69 kV.
quotes: Bright-line applicability rules are necessary to ensure developers have sufficient certainty regarding when FERC vs. state jurisdictional interconnection procedures will apply.
A higher threshold, such as 75-100 MW would be consistent with Eolian's project development experience.

letters.desc: ETX endorses the 20 MW threshold as necessary and practical. For hybrid projects, it recommends FERC also weigh the load-to-generation ratio to prevent applicants from packaging oversized stand-alone generation with a small load component to game the threshold.
quotes: The 20 MW threshold is necessary and practical.
For Hybrid projects, the Commission should consider both absolute size of the load (greater or equal to the threshold) and the relative size of the load component to the generation component.
A threshold lower than 20 MW could be manipulated to gain favorable treatment of oversized (effectively stand-alone) generation resources included in a Hybrid application.

letters.desc: Fervo supports the 20 MW threshold as appropriately tailored and consistent with existing LGIP and LGIA frameworks, ensuring procedural consistency and predictability for large-load and hybrid customers.
quotes: a 20 MW threshold is reasonable, appropriately tailored to the types of high-impact projects this rulemaking is intended to address, and fully consistent with the structure of the existing pro forma LGIP and LGIA

The LGIP framework is the Commission's established mechanism for studying and processing generation interconnection requests that can materially affect transmission system reliability. Aligning the applicability threshold for large-load and hybrid interconnections with this framework can ensure procedural consistency, reduce administrative complexity for transmission providers, and create a predictable pathway for customers whose system impacts are similar to those of large generators.

letters.desc: FirstEnergy argues that any rule should cover only data center customers at 200 MW or above. Including all loads at 20 MW risks clogging the queue, imposing burdens on non-data-center industrial customers, and undermining manufacturing and job-creation goals.
quotes: if the Commission elects to promulgate a rule for the interconnection of large load data center interconnections, it should do so in a targeted manner.
the Commission should limit any rule to (1) data centers that (2) have loads of at least 200 MW.
Sweeping in all large loads of 20 MW and above risks clogging interconnection queues, creating long interconnection wait times, and threatening the expedient interconnection of new data center load.

Imposing a 20 MW large load interconnection threshold also may result in prohibitory costs and onerous regulatory hurdles for other types of load customers, harming economic development that relies on the efficient and cost-effective interconnection of manufacturers and other traditional large load customers.

letters.desc: FirstEnergy urges raising the threshold to 200 MW and limiting the rule to data center customers. It argues a 20 MW floor sweeps in manufacturers and industrial loads that are not the source of today's grid pressure and would harm job growth and community investment.
quotes: the Commission should increase the ANOPR's tentatively proposed threshold of 20 MW to at least 200 MW because doing so will prevent the final rule from frustrating the goals of the ANOPR by adversely affecting industrial, manufacturing and other large load customers who are not the intended targets of the rule
A low megawatt threshold for jurisdictional load interconnections may unintentionally propagate economic risk and instability in communities searching for economic certainty and stability.

letters.desc: The filing argues that if a 20 MW threshold is adopted, it must clearly define how that threshold is measured for hybrids. Measuring at the point of interconnection could mask the true system impact when generation and load offset one another.
quotes: Adopting a separate interconnection standard for hybrid facilities that reflects each facility's actual operational characteristics and impact on the transmission grid, instead of applying the thresholds established for generation or load facilities

a separate standard is necessary for hybrid facilities that combine significant generation and load components. This distinction is critical because the generation component of a hybrid facility may exceed 20 MW and serve an associated load of comparable or greater magnitude, while the net output of the facility could appear to fall below 20 MW

letters.org: Georgia Power CompanyAlabama Power CompanyMississippi Power Company ,
letters.desc: The filer supports requiring large loads to cover the full costs of serving them so that existing retail customers do not bear the burden of new interconnections. They cite minimum bill requirements and termination provisions as effective tools already in use in the Southeast.
quotes: Doing so in a manner that ensures the reliability of the grid and appropriately allocates costs across customer classes is also crucially important to ensure the fast-moving nature of this demand growth does not create an undue risk that existing retail customers would subsidize a large load that seeks interconnection.

A combination of minimum bill requirements, termination provisions, and longer contract terms can help to ensure that data centers and other large load customers pay the full cost of serving them and avoid any risk that existing retail customers, particularly working families, seniors and small businesses, will be left to bear the costs.

letters.desc: The filing recommends setting the large-load threshold at 100 MW or above to focus the process on the loads actually driving demand growth. Objective viability criteria including site control and permit applications should serve as gating or prioritization requirements.
quotes: There is no reason to believe that exclusively relying on study deposits, withdrawal penalties, or other financial indications of readiness will be sufficient to deter the submission of requests by speculative or immature projects.

Geronimo Power believes that it is critical that any large load interconnection process adopted by the Commission incorporate objective and technology neutral criteria to ensure that large loads are prioritized based on their maturity and ability to come online in the near term.

Geronimo Power recommends the Commission apply a threshold that is set at a reasonable level that aligns with the size of the large loads that are driving this unprecedented load growth (e.g., 100 MW and above).
the Commission should require large loads to demonstrate that they have applied for material permits necessary for the construction of the large load's facility.

letters.desc: Google supports an MW-level threshold that triggers interconnection requirements uniformly across all new large loads, and opposes rules that single out specific end-uses such as data centers.
quotes: The Commission's reforms should apply uniformly to all new large loads (above a certain MW-level threshold) that seek to interconnect to the transmission system, regardless of end-use sector.

letters.desc: The IL OAG does not object to a 20 MW threshold and supports matching it to generator interconnection rules. It notes PJM and ComEd are considering 50 MW, but argues the real test is operational characteristics such as 24/7 operation, high voltage service, and concentrated demand.
quotes: large load interconnection requests accounted for only 80 MW in 2019, but jumped to 652 MW in 2022, to 3,931 MW in 2024, and to an astonishing 8,272 MW in 2025.

Whether a 20 MW or a 50 MW threshold is appropriate, the key factors are whether the large load customer has 24/7 operations, requires service at high voltage, presents high levels of concentrated demand, or has other characteristics that indicate that it should be included in the customer class that has direct effects on federal markets and the bulk power system.

letters.desc: The filer argues the ANOPR's 20 MW threshold is far too low and would drag in manufacturers, hospitals, and other non-data-center loads. They propose a 200 MW floor applied only to data center facilities, citing industry data showing that typical modern facilities already exceed that level. A lower threshold would clog the interconnection queue and undermine the ANOPR's own efficiency goals.
quotes: The Commission should limit the scope of any rule to data center facilities 200 MW or greater.
A 20 MW threshold would sweep in numerous load customers for which the ANOPR was not designed.

any rule adopted by the Commission should be limited to data center facilities, i.e. facilities that primarily utilize energy-consuming information equipment, as opposed to other types of large load customers.

A 20 MW threshold would sweep in a multitude of load customers with a highly diverse set of characteristics, including manufacturing facilities, commercial businesses, and municipal load-serving entities.

letters.desc: The filer argues the 20 MW ANOPR threshold is too low and should be raised substantially, to at least 200 MW, and limited to data center customers. A broader definition sweeps in industrial and commercial customers with different needs and would make interconnection less efficient for everyone.
quotes: it is in the best interest of the Commission and all stakeholders to adopt a reasonably narrow definition that confines the application of the rules to the types of customers driving the ANOPR:  large data center loads.

the Commission should focus this rulemaking on data center customers that are driving the largest load additions and contributing to network upgrades, and not adopt a threshold so low that it undermines efficiency and adversely impacts traditional industrial and commercial load customers.

Applying generic rules to a broad swathe of large load customers will likely end up making load interconnections more inefficient, both for data center customers as well as traditional industrial and commercial customers that often have very different technical, financial, and regulatory needs.

letters.desc: The filer supports establishing a minimum fault-level capacity threshold and a megawatt threshold above which large-load interconnection applications must pass preliminary fault-level screening. This ties eligibility to node characteristics rather than queue position, and provides a pathway for developers to proceed at disqualified nodes by committing to fund required upgrades.
quotes: The structural risk is not that demand will collapse. It is that siting decisions made on peak-trajectory assumptions will be exposed by a demand moderation that arrives faster than the infrastructure committed to serve it.

FERC should initiate a rulemaking establishing fault-level adequacy as a condition of large-load interconnection eligibility, with technical specifications derived from IEEE standards long applied by utilities to large industrial load interconnections.

letters.desc: IFP accepts full cost responsibility for large loads as appropriate given their capitalization levels, viewing it as a reasonable threshold condition for interconnection.
quotes: Principle 8 proposes that large loads should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades assigned to them. This is appropriate because – though it places an additional financial burden on the large loads – such loads are well capitalized and this cost is small compared to the overall costs of their projects.

letters.desc: ISO-NE supports a 20 MW threshold but wants FERC to specify how load is measured (maximum, average, or other) and at what point. It also argues that phased projects should be studied at their full aggregate MW to capture total system impact.
quotes: ISO-NE is generally supportive of applying a MW threshold for the application of a FERC-jurisdictional interconnection process.  A MW threshold, however, should be clearly defined.  For example, is the proposed 20 MW threshold based on the maximum load, average load, or something else, and where is the load level measured?

rules for interconnection of large loads should address interconnection of projects in stages.  For example, consider a large load customer's proposal to interconnect 30 MW in two stages of 15 MW each.  ISO-NE submits that the aggregate total of 30 MW should be captured in the supporting interconnection study to fully evaluate the system impacts of the total amount of load

letters.desc: ITC proposes raising the large load threshold from 20 MW to 50-100 MW to focus resources on projects with genuine material grid impact and avoid unnecessary delays to smaller projects. The higher threshold better reflects the operational scale of modern data centers and industrial loads.
quotes: ITC recommends the Commission consider raising the threshold for what constitutes a large load. In ITC's experience, the proposed threshold of 20 MW may capture a range of projects that are unlikely to have significant impacts on the broader grid, and which may in fact be slowed by a process intended for the unprecedently large loads that are now being proposed for immediate construction.

a threshold of 50 to 100 MW may be more appropriate and administratively manageable. This would also reflect the real operational differences between even quite large conventional retail and industrial load versus the recent proliferation of data center, crypto mining, or other extremely large loads which can shift tens or hundreds of megawatts in seconds.
A higher demand threshold would align resources with projects that have material system impact and avoid unintended backlogs and delays.

letters.desc: LPPC notes that member tariffs define qualifying large load customers by minimum power demand thresholds ranging from 5 MW to 75 or more MW, supporting the use of size-based eligibility to apply special terms only to the largest customers.
quotes: Defines the type of large load customer that qualifies, such as a minimum power demand (ranging from 5 MW to 75+ MW across LPPC members).

letters.desc: The filer cites examples from Norway and Idaho where capacity thresholds trigger differentiated charges or tariffs for large loads, and supports similar size-based rules to distinguish riskier large load connections from smaller ones.
quotes: socialising connection charges ("shallow charges") means that the connecting party (i.e. a data centre) does not pay the full cost of the network upgrades, so these are instead borne by other grid users (e.g. residential users).
Going in the opposite direction, Norway established in their latest policy update that a deep connection charge would be used for projects with capacity above 1 MW.

letters.desc: Meta proposes raising the minimum MW threshold for large load interconnection reform from the ANOPR's proposed 20 MW to 75 MW or higher, arguing that 20 MW does not accurately target loads that would benefit from reform.
quotes: Data center developers and other sources of large load need faster, transparent, and more predictable interconnection processes

In Meta's experience, that threshold is too low and would not accurately target the large loads that would most benefit from reform of interconnection processes. Meta proposes that the Commission instead consider a threshold of 75 MW or higher

letters.desc: The filer opposes a definition of large load based solely on MW size. They favor a flexible standard that accounts for operational, reliability, and administrative factors, consistent with the approach being developed through MISO's stakeholder process.
quotes: the MISO Transmission Owners generally support a definition that avoids a threshold based solely on the MW size of the load and instead provides reasonable flexibility in defining large loads, given the technical experience and judgment that is required to appropriately and reasonably weigh operational, reliability, and administrative factors that are critical to defining large loads.

letters.org: North Carolina Utilities Commission Public Staff
letters.desc: If FERC proceeds, the Public Staff recommends limiting any rule to loads above 300 MW to reduce the number of customers studied, focus on bulk-system impacts, and lessen jurisdictional concerns.
quotes: the North Carolina Public Staff recommends that if the Commission promulgates a rule on large load interconnection, that it limit its applicability to loads in excess of 300 MW.

letters.org: Office of the Ohio Consumers' Counsel
letters.desc: OCC supports a defined 20 MW minimum threshold to limit federal jurisdiction to the largest transmission-connected loads, preserve state oversight of smaller customers, and require public posting for requests at or above that level.
quotes: All interconnection requests above 20 MW, including project type and location
OCC supports retaining a defined minimum threshold such as 20 MW for purposes of any federal interconnection standard.

letters.desc: Ohio FEA supports FERC establishing a clear MW threshold for federal jurisdiction over data center interconnections, recommending 20-25 MW for consistency with generator interconnection precedent.
quotes: the Ohio FEA supports the adoption of a clear threshold at which such federal jurisdiction would be invoked

In AEP Ohio's data center tariff, the PUCO established a threshold of 25 MW for inclusion in the new customer class. However, for consistency with generator interconnections, 20 MW could also be a reasonable threshold.

letters.desc: OpenAI proposes that DOE designate loads above 250 MW with national-interest, security, economic, or critical-infrastructure value for expedited treatment.
quotes: OpenAI supports an approach that allows the DOE to identify and provide a "national-interest" designation for loads above 250 MW that have clear national interest or security,economicimperativeorcompetitiveness,orcritical-infrastructurevalue

letters.desc: PG&E supports limiting the final rule to new loads above 20 MW, and strongly urges that customers who have already submitted interconnection applications be grandfathered under existing rules to avoid mid-process disruption.
quotes: To avoid delays and the uncertainty of potential mid-stream changes, PG&E strongly recommends that the Commission make clear that a final rule will only apply to large load customers who have not yet submitted an interconnection application to a utility and/or transmission provider as of the date of the Commission issues a decision.

PG&E recommends that large load customers that submit interconnection applications/requests prior to the effective date of the final rule be allowed to proceed under the rules and requirements in place at the time the interconnection request was submitted.

letters.desc: JCA argue that the sheer volume and pace of large load interconnection requests constitute special circumstances under existing FERC policy, warranting a departure from the standard higher-of rule without necessarily requiring a formal rate policy change.
quotes: Special circumstances exist today due to the high volume of large load customers seeking to interconnect to the transmission system and the speed to power demanded by them, requiring significant network facilities to be constructed near immediately.

letters.org: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer AdvocateDelaware Division of the Public Advocate
letters.desc: The filers endorse the ANOPR's 20 MW threshold and specify it should apply to the customer's aggregate power requirement across all points of interconnection to prevent splitting loads to avoid coverage.
quotes: The Joint Consumer Advocates support the ANOPR's minimum threshold of 20 megawatts (MW) for both large loads and hybrid facilities, and this threshold should apply to the customer's aggregate power requirement rather than to a single point of interconnection.

letters.org: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer AdvocateDelaware Division of the Public AdvocateIllinois Office of Attorney General ,
letters.desc: The filers support the proposed 20 MW threshold and oppose raising it, arguing a lower threshold protects against reliability risks and deters evasion. They also argue the threshold should apply to a customer's aggregate demand and to planned full operational capacity rather than initial or per-point capacity.
quotes: treating new large loads differently from other load is reasonable and necessary to ensure reliable service and just and reasonable rates for existing consumers, especially residential consumers

FERC can and must appropriately treat new large loads attributable to data centers differently from other kinds of load because: (1) data centers are creating unique difficulties for the grid and impacting a uniquely vulnerable market at a uniquely expensive level; and (2) investments in data centers can be speculative and uncertain in nature, increasing the risk of a severe market correction that would create stranded costs.

FERC should stay the course and adopt the proposed 20 MW threshold to define large loads and hybrid facilities because this MW threshold helps protect against reliability concerns from large loads or hybrid facilities by requiring proper interconnection studies that will reduce reliability risks for all electricity consumers.
the threshold 'should apply to the customer's aggregate power requirement rather than to a single point of interconnection.'

The definition of large load and hybrid facilities should use the planned full operational capacity, even if the facility is planning to ramp up its operations over time. Otherwise, a new large load or hybrid facility could circumvent the threshold requirement by phasing in its operations.

letters.org: PSEG CompaniesPSEG Energy Resources & Trade LLCPSEG Power LLC ,Public Service Electric and Gas Company ,
letters.desc: PSEG argues the proposed 20 MW threshold is too low and would inadvertently cover distribution-level commercial loads outside FERC jurisdiction. It recommends increasing the threshold to at least 30 MW, noting the average U.S. data center already exceeds 40 MW.
quotes: the Commission should increase the 20 MW threshold to 30 MW or greater to avoid pulling in non-data center customers or other commercial customers who were not intended to be covered by the ANOPR.

letters.desc: Shell Energy agrees a minimum MW threshold is necessary and should be set high enough to limit administrative burden while low enough, when combined with deposits, to capture total load additions that affect resource adequacy and wholesale prices. Regional stakeholder processes should determine the exact level.
quotes: At the time of entry into load queue, Shell Energy supports study deposits, readiness requirements including application fees, and withdrawal penalties for load interconnection requests similar to existing generator interconnections studies and application fees.

letters.desc: Terraflux supports applying the reforms to loads and hybrid facilities above 20MW, consistent with LGIP generation thresholds.
quotes: We agree with the second principle's assertion that reforms should apply to new loads greater than 20MW and new hybrid facilities greater than 20MW, aligned with FERC's generation thresholds of the LGIP

letters.desc: TBA agrees the 20 MW threshold for FERC jurisdiction is appropriate given existing large generator interconnection precedent, and supports non-firm service options for flexible loads above that threshold.
quotes: Flexible loads that select non-firm service and can avoid peak loads should receive reduced interconnection and transmission upgrade requirements, and should avoid all network resource and resource adequacy/capacity requirements.

letters.desc: TBA recommends that non-firm service eligibility be tied to tangible operational characteristics such as thermal storage capacity, process flexibility, or battery backing, rather than self-reported flexibility claims.
quotes: non-firm eligibility must be tied to tangible operational characteristics

letters.desc: The filer identifies open questions on how much load must be curtailable, how many hours, what response times, and whether commitments are firm. It urges objective criteria to avoid inconsistent standards and regulatory uncertainty, and asks FERC to account for regional differences.
quotes: On the load side, major considerations include the percentage of load that must be curtailable, how many hours annually a load must be flexible, what response times are required, and whether curtailability commitments must be firm or may be conditional on operational constraints.
Without objective criteria, transmission providers will apply inconsistent standards, and developers will face regulatory uncertainty that undermines the benefits of expedited processing.
The Commission should also be open considering and taking stock of regional differences on these issues.

letters.org: Utility Intervention Unit, New York State Department of Stat
letters.desc: The UIU supports applying cost-causation principles so that each large load project bears the incremental cost of the upgrades it requires, with shared benefits rigorously quantified before any cost is allocated to others.
quotes: Each large load project's cost responsibility must reflect the incremental cost of required local and network upgrades, ensuring that large load developers fund the infrastructure needed to support their own demand.

letters.desc: Verrus asks FERC to define a flexible load subclass requiring physical on-site assets (battery storage, power-flow controls) that enable sustained, dispatchable flexibility over the life of the interconnection. The threshold should require a material share of load (e.g., 20 MW or 25%) be curtailable to meet NERC reserve standards.
quotes: The Commission should establish a clear, standardized definition of 'flexible load' as an asset-backed, verifiable, and dispatchable demand capable of modulating consumption in coordination with the transmission provider or balancing authority throughout a long-term commitment.

Flexibility must be physical, durable, and measurable—not merely theoretical or price-responsive. The defining characteristic should be the presence of on-site assets such as battery energy storage, power-flow controls, or other infrastructure that enables sustained, repeatable flexibility over decades, not just seasonal participation.

letters.desc: Verrus proposes that loads qualify for the flexible subclass by committing to curtail the greater of 20 MW or 25% of total load, anchored to Order No. 2003 precedent for defining a large generator. The filing opposes requiring 100% curtailability, arguing partial curtailment of a large load still provides substantial system relief.
quotes: a load should qualify for the "Flexible" subclass (and the associated fast-lane study) if it commits to curtailing the greater of 20 MW or 25% of its total load.

Insisting on 100% curtailability would strand significant value. A facility that can curtail 50% or even 25% of a massive load could still offer hundreds of megawatts of relief to the system—relief that can avoid upgrades and improve reliability.

letters.desc: The filer supports a size threshold in principle but argues the 20 MW figure in the ANOPR is well below existing state benchmarks of 70 to 75 MW. A voltage threshold might make an MW floor unnecessary; if one is kept, it should be set higher and include anti-evasion rules for incremental load additions.
quotes: Should FERC assert its jurisdiction over large load interconnection, it must clearly limit its jurisdiction to large loads connecting to transmission facilities as suggested in the ANOPR. However, reliance on the 'seven factor test' alone is insufficient to avoid potential uncertainty at the boundary of state and federal jurisdiction, which could cause unnecessary delay and added cost to the large load interconnection process, contrary to DOE's stated goal of achieving speed to power.

United suggests that one potential approach to clarifying when a FERC-jurisdictional large load jurisdiction process should apply is to establish a rebuttable presumption that any large load interconnection above a certain voltage threshold is defined as interconnecting to a 'transmission facility' subject to FERC jurisdiction for purposes of large load interconnections.

United notes that the 20 MW threshold put forward in the ANOPR is significantly lower than the definition of 'large load' already in use in states that have taken action to standardize large load interconnections. For example, Texas statute defines large load as any load above 75 MW, and the recent Indiana & Michigan power settlement defined large load customer as a customer with contract capacity greater than or equal to 70 MW at an individual plant.

letters.desc: ATC opposes the 20 MW size threshold as too broad, arguing it would capture ordinary non-data-center loads and overwhelm study resources. Instead, ATC recommends thresholds tied to operating behavior: ramp rate, active power oscillation, and low-voltage ride-through capability.
quotes: a 20 MW threshold would be too low and too vague for implementing load interconnection procedures.  A 20 MW threshold would include many existing and future non-data center loads.  This over-inclusivity would lead to unwieldy procedures and unintended consequences, including overwhelming study resources and likely delaying interconnecting the very loads that the Commission is seeking to expedite.
ATC recommends that the Commission consider adopting an applicability threshold based upon load behavior.

the Commission should consider adopting threshold applicability requirements based upon specific operating requirements for all loads in terms of ramp rates (i.e., how quickly they can increase or decrease electricity usage), active power oscillatory behavior (i.e., how much and how fast active power can swing once they are online), and ride-through capability (i.e., how well the load can remain connected and stable during grid disturbances such as voltage dips, frequency excursions, or short interruptions).

letters.desc: DPN treats 20 MW as an adequate baseline but wants exceptions for smaller facilities such as hydro that fall below the limit, so developers can start small and expand.
quotes: in certain cases, it should expand to facilities below 20 MW given that hydro facilities can often fall under this capacity limit.

letters.desc: EEI opposes the 20 MW default threshold as too low and too broad, arguing it would capture traditional industrial customers outside the ANOPR's intent. EEI proposes a minimum national default of 100 MW while allowing regional variation downward based on local system characteristics.
quotes: the 20 MW threshold is inappropriate for the specific, high-impact load customers that the ANOPR is intending to address. If the Commission adopts a universal default or threshold definition of large load customers premised on that customer's (gross) peak demand, it should be no lower than 100 MW, allowing for flexibility to reflect the unique circumstances of the region.

the potential clarity and ease of a universal threshold for large load would likely be outweighed by over- or under-inclusion of impactful large load with corresponding high costs for inadequate improvement to [bulk power system] reliability.

letters.desc: ENGIE does not take a firm position on 20 MW but warns it may capture mid-size commercial facilities that pose no system risk, increasing regulatory burden. ENGIE recommends letting regions set their own thresholds through transparent stakeholder processes.
quotes: While ENGIE does not take a strong view on whether 20 MW is the appropriate threshold, we suggest that the 20 MW threshold may be too low for the types of large loads that typically drive new transmission needs.

ENGIE recommends that the Commission allow for flexibility in implementation of a given megawatt threshold by deferring to the regions in setting a reasonable threshold. The Commission should require that ISOs and RTOs conduct a transparent stakeholder process to determine an appropriate threshold while relying on relevant system and queue data.

letters.desc: Entergy opposes the proposed 20 MW threshold as too low, arguing it would sweep in speculative projects and dilute any rule's effectiveness. It recommends 100 MW and notes broad commenter consensus that 75 to 100 MW is appropriate. It also rejects voltage-based proxies as introducing unnecessary delay and complexity.
quotes: any threshold lower than 75-100 MW is more likely to capture speculative projects and could result in a Final Rule so broad that it would render it ineffective and reduce or eliminate any efficiencies that would otherwise be gained
the consensus among commentors is that increasing the threshold above 20 MW, to an amount of 75 MW-100 MW, would suffice

letters.desc: The filer suggests a voltage or MW threshold well above 20 MW could let transmission providers require only the largest loads to use a federal process, but cautions that any fixed threshold invites loads to artificially reduce capacity below the line, causing greater inefficiency.
quotes: the Commission could consider a voltage or MW threshold (likely much greater than 20 MW) such that transmission providers could still require the largest loads to participate in a federal interconnection process.
any specific threshold may result in loads artificially reducing their capacity to just below that threshold to avoid such requirements, which could result in greater inefficiencies overall.

letters.desc: The commenter accepts the 20 MW threshold concept but flags two gaps: hybrid facilities whose gross load far exceeds their net interconnection amount, and modular load facilities that fragment below the threshold at a shared point. Anti-fragmentation aggregation rules are recommended.
quotes: if a hybrid facility has 100MW of load and 80MW of generation (to have a sum total of 20MW), they can provide an outsized threat to the grid if one day they simply turn off their on-site generators to slam the full 100MW load onto the grid.

Can you clarify whether modular loads (e.g., phased data centers with multiple 10–15 MW modules) that individually fall below 20 MW but share a POI will be aggregated? Recommend anti‑fragmentation rules that aggregate affiliated requests within a time and facility/geographic window.

letters.desc: iMasons argues that the ANOPR's proposed 20 MW threshold is too low given that modern data centers often exceed hundreds of MWs or even 1 GW, and recommends a minimum of 75 MW or higher.
quotes: iMasons believes that a minimum threshold of 75 MW (or potentially higher) is appropriate for the Commission to consider.

letters.desc: LS Power supports the 20 MW threshold direction but calls for a substantive comment period to develop a clearer standard, whether based on grid impact or load megawatts, and to address regional variations and the meaning of 'new' load.
quotes: New large load must be well-defined. The Commission must define it clearly, based on an agreed upon standard, such as whether new large load would have a significant impact to the transmission and energy supply system or based upon load megawatts.

letters.desc: MISO opposes a purely size-based national threshold for defining large load, noting that grid impacts vary by location and density. MISO recommends a hybrid approach combining NERC registration categories with RTO-specific minimum thresholds.
quotes: a universal definition of "large load" should not be based solely on size.  Instead, MISO recommends a hybrid approach to determining what constitutes a "large load."  The hybrid approach could consist of: (i) NERC registration or NERC Reliability Standards development; and (ii) allowing ISO/RTOs to determine specific minimum thresholds to support market registration and application processes that fit the unique needs of their footprints.

letters.desc: PJM questions whether 20 MW is the right cutoff, noting that most data centers far exceed that level and a lower threshold could over-capture loads, clog the queue, and defeat the ANOPR's speed goals.
quotes: Even assuming record evidence could support the ANOPR's proposed 20 MW load threshold for the ANOPR's conceptual reforms to apply, is that clear line set at the appropriate level given that large loads, most especially data centers, tend to be substantially larger than 20 MW?  Will such a threshold over capture load subject to the proposed reforms, clog interconnection processes, and stymie the intended proposed reforms?

letters.desc: SMA asks FERC to allow modular inverter-BESS systems to be aggregated when applying the 20 MW performance threshold, reflecting how data center racks scale up incrementally. The connection capacity at the point of interconnection, not the rating of a single unit, is the relevant metric.
quotes: The performance threshold should be defined to include advanced grid-forming inverters combined with BESS, which may need to be aggregated to exceed 20 MW (in line with the modular build-up of data center racks).

letters.desc: SEIA wants storage excluded from the rule and questions whether 20 MW is the right cutoff, noting that a NERC survey found most respondents defined 'large' as over 50 MW. SEIA asks the Commission to gather data on actual load sizes and demand profiles before fixing a threshold, and recommends adding a voltage criterion alongside the MW threshold.
quotes: The Commission must make clear that grid-charging energy storage resources should not be considered load under any potential rulemaking.

In order to set a legally defensible size for which loads are considered 'large,' the Commission should request data on the average size of new large loads, as well as the demand profiles and curtailment abilities, of those loads.

letters.org: Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group
letters.desc: The SPP TO Group supports SPP's voltage-tiered threshold (10 MW at 69 kV or below; 50 MW above 69 kV) rather than the ANOPR's flat 20 MW cutoff. The filer accepts that other regions may justify different thresholds but asks FERC not to mandate a single number.
quotes: the threshold SPP adopted in its HILL reform varies by voltage.  Specifically, A new commercial or industrial load, or increase in commercial or industrial load, at a single site connected through one or more shared Points of Interconnection (POIs) or delivery points, where such load is either (1) 10 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a voltage level less than or equal to 69 [kilovolts (kV)]; or (2) 50 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a voltage level greater than 69 kV.

While a 20 MW threshold may work for other regions, it would not work for SPP.  However, transmission providers outside of SPP should be left to define 'large loads' as they see fit with their stakeholders and according to their region's unique circumstances.  The Commission need not dictate what the limit is, although it should direct all transmission providers to designate and justify an appropriate threshold.

letters.desc: ACP opposes the proposed 20MW threshold, arguing it is unrealistically low and would sweep many mid-sized, low-risk projects into federal jurisdiction that already have predictable pathways under current rules. Recommends a significantly higher threshold, ideally 100MW or higher.
quotes: the proposed 20 MW load threshold (ANOPR Principle 2) may be unrealistically low for the types of large loads that drive transmission needs, and could inadvertently increase uncertainty by sweeping an unnecessarily high number of load interconnection requests into a new process Federal jurisdiction.

By contrast, a 20MW standalone threshold would capture many mid-sized projects that may pose little system risk, and in many cases may have a predictable pathway to interconnection under current rules.

ACP recommends that the Commission utilize the record developed in this proceeding to establish a load interconnection threshold significantly higher than 20MW, while also taking note of multiple load interconnections at the same grid connection point that could be individually lower but collectively higher than the threshold level.

letters.desc: APS argues the 20 MW threshold for large loads is set too low and should be increased.
quotes: APS does believe that the 20 MW threshold for what is considered a large load could be increased.

letters.desc: The CPUC rejects any federal threshold over retail load but argues that if one is set it must be far above 20 MW, which would sweep in small commercial and industrial loads not intended to be covered. The 20 MW figure appears borrowed from generator interconnection rather than actual data center load profiles in California.
quotes: This analogy between generator and large-load interconnections is too simplistic and does not account for fundamental jurisdictional and technical distinctions established under the FPA.

The CPUC is concerned that a threshold as low as 20 MW for large load energization will ensnare small commercial and industrial load in a large load energization process, which is not the intended goal of the ANOPR.

while reiterating that there is no appropriate threshold for federal oversight of retail large load energizations, if a threshold is established, the CPUC believes that it should be far greater than 20 MW.

letters.desc: CEBA opposes the proposed 20 MW threshold as too low and recommends 75 MW instead. At 20 MW, the rule would capture mid-sized industrial and commercial facilities traditionally regulated by states, overwhelming FERC and creating wholesale-retail boundary disputes.
quotes: CEBA recommends substantially increasing the threshold to avoid overburdening the large load interconnection process. A new standard, such as a 75 MW threshold instead of 20 MW, would ensure that FERC is focusing its attention and resources on loads that have greater system impact.

A 20 MW cutoff, for example, is too low: it would capture many mid-sized industrial and commercial facilities (factories, hospitals, campuses) traditionally under state jurisdiction, creating tension with state regulators and blurring wholesale vs. retail boundaries.

letters.desc: The filer contends the proposed 20 MW threshold is far too low and would capture ordinary retail customers unrelated to data centers. Consumers Energy recommends a 100 MW nationwide threshold to keep any reforms narrowly targeted to the problem the ANOPR seeks to address.
quotes: a 20 MW threshold for load interconnections would capture a myriad of customers that come nowhere close to the data centers and other major industrial loads driving the ANOPR's proposed reforms.
Consumers Energy submits that a 100 MW nationwide threshold would be more appropriate than the ANOPR's 20 MW proposal.

letters.desc: Duke Energy opposes the proposed 20 MW threshold as far too low, recommending 300 MW (minimum 100 MW) at 100 kV or above, further narrowed to loads with NERC-identified reliability characteristics. The 20 MW level would sweep in conventional industrial and commercial loads that utilities have served for decades without issue.
quotes: Duke Energy recommends that, for purposes of this rulemaking, FERC define large load as new loads greater than 300 MW (but, in the alternative, no lower than 100 MW), that require interconnection at 100 kilovolt (kV) or above.
A threshold of 20 MW would capture conventional larger loads including manufacturing, commercial, and other industrial loads, which can average around 50 MW in size.

letters.desc: EEI and other commenters find the ANOPR's proposed 20 MW threshold too low, as it would capture many ordinary industrial and commercial customers rather than focusing on high-impact data centers. EEI supports a higher threshold that can be adjusted by region to account for local system conditions.
quotes: EEI notes that many commenters considered the 20 MW threshold suggested by the ANOPR to be too low.
commenters agreed that a 20 MW threshold would fail to ensure that reforms are focused on the high-impact data center customers that provided the impetus for the ANOPR.
any nominal threshold should be subject to adjustment to reflect regional and local concerns.

letters.desc: ELCON opposes a bright-line MW threshold as too blunt to capture the varied characteristics of new large loads. The Commission should instead survey existing regional protocols and tailor rules to actual bottlenecks, allowing regions with adequate procedures to demonstrate compliance without wholesale replacement.
quotes: Rather than instituting an arbitrary MW threshold, the Commission should understand what load interconnection protocols have already been established in certain regions and tailor principles to address the bottlenecks that are specific to new large loads and their electricity needs.
responsible entities should be provided with an opportunity to demonstrate that its current rules and procedures meet or exceed any Commission guidelines.

letters.desc: ECA opposes using a 230 kV voltage threshold as a jurisdictional cutoff, arguing it would exclude much of the FERC-jurisdictional system, leave regulatory gaps, and could incentivize lower-voltage construction to avoid requirements. ECA prefers the existing seven-factor test.
quotes: Other customers lack sufficient transparency into how costs are incurred and allocated and in forecasts of new large loads to have confidence that investments made to serve new large loads are not being shifted to them or exposing them to stranded cost risk.
ECA believes continued reliance on the long-standing seven-factor test is appropriate, legally sound, and will not materially increase litigation challenges.
A voltage threshold (especially one as high as 230 kV) will be an incomplete remedy to the risks to just and reasonable rates driving the need for Commission action and leave regulatory gaps.

letters.desc: Entergy opposes the proposed 20 MW threshold as too low. A 20 MW threshold would quadruple the number of qualifying loads in Entergy territories, create administrative overload, and invite speculative projects. Entergy recommends at least 100 MW, consistent with thresholds used by the White House EO, Georgia PSC, and other state programs.
quotes: Entergy Services urges the Commission to consider alternative thresholds above 20 MW and recommend a threshold of at least 100 MW.  Anything less than a 100 MW threshold invites inefficiency, delay, and the potential for speculative projects to attempt to take advantage of any expedited process provided for under a final rule.

reducing the MW threshold for what is considered a 'large load' in each service territory from 100 MW to 20 MW, would increase the number of existing customers that would qualify as a large load under the proposed ANOPR by more than four times.

letters.org: Governor Josh Shapiro and Governor Glenn Youngkin
letters.desc: The governors argue the 20 MW threshold as proposed would substantially pull loads that have traditionally been regulated by states into federal jurisdiction. They call for further public process to settle the right size and characteristics for triggering shared jurisdiction.
quotes: we believe that the limit as proposed would substantially impact traditional state jurisdiction over loads.
We look forward to further public participation on what characteristics and size best serve to implicate shared state and federal jurisdiction in this regard.

letters.org: Industrial Energy Consumers of America et al.
letters.desc: The filers argue the proposed 20 MW threshold is arbitrary and far too low, capturing manufacturers that are not driving today's grid challenges. They recommend a minimum threshold of 75 MW to 100 MW, applied only to new loads, and suggest using FERC's Seven Factor Test or NERC's bulk electric system definition rather than a bright-line MW figure.
quotes: mandating all new loads greater than 20 MW to go through a separate, new, federal process could cause significant negative impacts, including: disrupting existing processes; triggering confusion between state and federal organizations and regulators; creating business uncertainty; and diverting limited and scarce resources from staff at the Commission, at RTOs/ISOs, and at public utilities.

the Industrial Customer Organizations believe a 20 MW limit is far too low and would capture a significant number of manufacturing entities and other industrial and institutional organizations that do not have the speed-to-market and scale demands that are primarily driving today's grid challenges.
If a threshold is set by the Commission, it should be at a minimum of 75 MW-100 MW (or higher), restricted to new load added to the grid, and with reasonable and clear aggregation rules.

letters.org: Industrial Energy Consumers of America et al.
letters.desc: The filers oppose a 20 MW threshold as too low, noting that newer data centers routinely exceed 500 MW and that the larger loads are driving unprecedented growth. They recommend using the Seven Factor Test instead of any fixed MW figure.
quotes: If FERC implements a standardized large load interconnection process and load queue, then the Commission should consider using FERC's Seven Factor Test to evaluate the jurisdictional nature of the interconnection, in lieu of any arbitrary MW threshold.

letters.desc: IECA argues the proposed 20 MW threshold is too low: for speed-to-market, expedited review should apply to all loads regardless of size; for reliability purposes, the 20 MW floor is inconsequential and a 100 MW floor is more meaningful.
quotes: for purposes of expediting interconnection to the transmissions system (i.e., enhancing "speed to market"), we submit that expedited review and approval should be available to all loads (i.e., all Data Centers), not just large Data Centers in excess of any particular size.

Reliability and resource adequacy issues are affected much more by loads of 100 MW or larger, so setting an artificially low threshold could be problematic for purposes of addressing grid reliability.

letters.desc: LPPC considers the 20 MW threshold too low and asks FERC to defer to regional variation, noting that ISOs and utilities have already set varied thresholds based on local grid characteristics.
quotes: LPPC asks the Commission to defer to varied regional approaches. Utilities across the country and ISOs/RTOs have set varied thresholds for the definition of large loads, based on judgments regarding grid configuration and available transmission capacity. LPPC is of the view that the 20 MW threshold is low, and that loads substantially larger than 20 MW have been integrated with some frequency under state-based protocols.

letters.org: Louisiana Public Service CommissionMississippi Public Service Commission
letters.desc: The 20 MW threshold would sweep in hundreds of thousands of loads, overwhelming FERC. The commissions urge a much higher threshold limited to loads where interconnection delays have actually been demonstrated.
quotes: The Louisiana and Mississippi Commissions suggest that 20 MW is too low and will result in FERC exercising interconnection jurisdiction over hundreds and thousands of new loads, far beyond FERC's capabilities of reasonably addressing.
The threshold should be far higher and set to only address larger loads that are shown to be affected by interconnection delays.

letters.desc: Maryland opposes FERC's proposed 20 MW threshold as insufficient. The state notes Maryland law sets 100 MW with 80% load factor, and PJM considers requests of 50 MW or larger. A higher and regionally flexible threshold allows smaller loads to access service through lower-risk avenues.
quotes: Setting a minimum load threshold can allow smaller load customers to receive service through other avenues, where the associated financial risks are not as significant
MEA recommends FERC consider a higher threshold than 20 MW for defining new load and hybrid facilities for the purposes of the proposal, and allow some flexibility to meet unique regional needs

letters.desc: Maryland law defines large load customers at 100 MW or more, far above the ANOPR's 20 MW threshold. The Maryland PSC warns that overlapping federal and state definitions would create regulatory confusion and could extend FERC requirements to retail customers never intended to be covered.
quotes: the Maryland legislature has established that a "large load customer" is a commercial or industrial customer (for retail electric service) that "has or is projected to have an aggregate monthly demand of at least 100 MW…." Where the ANOPR would prescribe new standards and requirements on large load customers that exceed the 20 MW threshold—a much lower qualifying threshold—the Maryland PSC is concerned that if FERC were to exercise jurisdiction over load, these inconsistencies in these large load definitions would create confusion in the regulatory space

letters.desc: The filer argues that a single MW threshold is too crude a measure for defining large loads, citing NERC guidance that footprint, ramp rates, protection systems, and other factors matter. They recommend that regional providers retain flexibility to set context-appropriate thresholds.
quotes: Should the Commission elect to pursue the reforms proposed in the ANOPR, the MISO Transmission Owners recommend that the Commission provide transmission providers and their stakeholders significant flexibility in defining large loads, as they have the technical experience and judgment to appropriately and reasonably weigh operational, reliability, and administrative factors that are critical to defining large loads.

a threshold based solely on the MW size of load is too rough of a measure when developing a large load definition.  As the North American Electric Reliability Corporation ("NERC") explained, several factors should also be considered, such as footprint, load ramp rates, real-time behavior and flexibility, protection systems, and backup power schemes.

letters.desc: The proposed 20 MW threshold lacks an evidentiary basis and could clog the process with small entities, discourage industrial expansion, and conflict with state retail tariffs. Any threshold should rest on evidence distinguishing large load profiles from ordinary load.
quotes: The proposed 20 MW threshold could be too low, potentially clogging the process with small entities, discouraging industrial expansion, and interfering with state retail tariffs. Load is not the same as generation, and any threshold should be based on evidence of different load profiles that would be subject to the rule.

letters.desc: The Market Monitor opposes the ANOPR's 20 MW threshold as an unjustified carry-over from generator rules. It recommends a threshold no higher than 5 MW to prevent gaming through disaggregation of data center interconnection points. A 200 MW cutoff is dismissed as an attempt to avoid the queue entirely.
quotes: There is no reason to simply extend the generator threshold to loads. Generators have generally been very large compared to individual loads. While there is no completely objective threshold for large new data center loads, the threshold should be no higher than five MW.
The suggestion that the cutoff for the load queue should be 200 MW is an attempt to avoid the issue, would miss many data centers and would permit gaming of the rules to avoid the queue.

letters.desc: National Grid opposes a uniform 20 MW bright-line threshold. In New York and New England, a threshold of 50 MW to 80 MW would be more appropriate to avoid pulling small projects into lengthy cluster study processes. Each region should set its own threshold.
quotes: A final rule should reflect this reality and be limited to truly large loads as defined on a region-by-region basis, which in most regions, including New York and New England, is likely to be at a higher MW threshold than 20 MW.

National Grid is concerned that a bright line 20 MW test for defining "large loads" will not be workable in many regions of the nation.  Such a low threshold could subject smaller projects with minimal reliability impact or required upgrades to a cluster study process or other large load interconnection process in the NYISO and ISO-NE regions that extends for a long time.

letters.desc: NRECA opposes a uniform 20 MW threshold applied nationwide, arguing many cooperatives view it as too low. The Commission should let regions propose higher thresholds and vary limits based on load characteristics and local system conditions.
quotes: NRECA agrees that a lower-bound size limit on 'large loads' is necessary, but it opposes uniform, nationwide interconnection rules for all loads greater than 20 MW, which many electric cooperatives believe is too low.

the Commission should allow regional flexibility to establish a higher MW threshold, as well as different limits for different load characteristics and different transmission system configurations and conditions.

letters.desc: The 20 MW threshold is too low and drastically increases covered entities. Many loads in the 20 to 50 MW range connect to distribution or subtransmission, not bulk transmission, and are outside FERC jurisdiction. A 50 MW threshold would focus on truly large loads with greatest transmission impact.
quotes: the 20 megawatt threshold in the ANOPR is too low. Such a small number drastically increases the number of entities that would be covered by the proposed rule.

many loads between 20 and 50 megawatts are not directly connected to the transmission system but rather are connected to distribution and sub-transmission system facilities that are not subject to FERC jurisdiction.
By increasing the threshold in any final rule to 50 megawatts the truly large loads that have the greatest impact on the transmission system would be covered.
for loads as small as 20 megawatts, one size does not fit all

letters.desc: The 20 MW threshold proposed in the ANOPR may be too low given the current surge in load requests. NMPRC recommends starting with a 50 MW minimum and examining whether it aligns with RTO initiatives.
quotes: Regarding the proposed minimum of 20 MW, this threshold may be too low at this time of an extremely large number of load requests. FERC should consider a larger threshold, and should consider if this threshold compliments, or conflicts with, similar initiatives being pursued by RTOs. The NMPRC suggests starting with a minimum threshold of 50 MW.

letters.org: New York Transmission OwnersCentral Hudson Gas & Electric CorporationNew York Power Authority ,New York State Electric & Gas Corp. and Rochester Gas and El ,Niagara Mohawk d/b/a/ National Grid ,Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. and Orange and ,Long Island Power Authority ,
letters.desc: The NYTOs oppose treating the 20 MW screen as a jurisdictional trigger for cost allocation or service classification. They argue the threshold was set in the generator interconnection context and should not be applied mechanically to large-load interconnections; regions need discretion to set thresholds reflecting voltage, topology, and local system characteristics. For cost allocation and option-to-build purposes, a higher threshold such as 100 MW is more appropriate.
quotes: The 20 MW screen in Principle 2 should be treated as a planning indicator, not a jurisdictional trigger, so that regions can tailor applicability based on voltage, topology, and reliability considerations.

States, regions, and each Transmission Owner must retain discretion to set triggers that reflect local system characteristics and each Transmission Owner must have discretion to determine whether each customer is interconnecting at the transmission or distribution level under FERC's seven factor test.
the Commission should focus any cost allocation and option to build rules on those large load customers likely requiring the most transmission improvements (e.g., at 100 MW).

letters.desc: NCUC expresses concern about the proposed 20 MW threshold without specifying an alternative. The concern appears to relate to how this threshold interacts with state jurisdiction over retail loads.
quotes: the NCUC is also concerned about the proposed 20 MW large load threshold

letters.desc: NREMC contends the 20 MW threshold is far too low and unfairly captures manufacturing and industrial loads that differ fundamentally from the hyper-concentrated data-center loads driving this proceeding. The cooperative urges a minimum threshold of 100 MW to focus the rules on the actual problem.
quotes: a uniform, nationwide bright-line standard at 20 MW is far too low and would include many manufacturing and industrial loads essential for communities across nation. These types of loads bear little resemblance in scale, behavior, or system impact to the concern driving this proceeding: extraordinarily large, highly concentrated data-center demand measured in the hundreds of megawatts or even gigawatts, at a single point of interconnection. The minimum threshold should more closely reflect these loads of concern and should be set at no less than 100 MW.

Smaller or more distributed loads present fundamentally different characteristics and risk profiles. Their electrical demands, operational behavior, and location on the system do not produce the same system-level challenges that hyper-concentrated data-center growth creates.

letters.desc: NRG contends the 20 MW threshold is borrowed arbitrarily from generator interconnection rules and has no jurisdictional logic when applied to loads. Small loads do not connect at transmission voltage, and the threshold could trap scaling data centers in state procedures even after they exceed the limit.
quotes: The 20 MW size restriction appears to be arbitrary.  This figure appears to have been selected as the threshold for large loads because it is the threshold for large generators subject to the Commission-prescribed large generator interconnection procedures, rather than the small generator interconnection procedures.
there are likely to be data centers and other large loads whose initial size will be below the 20 MW threshold but which will ramp up in size over time.

letters.desc: ODEC opposes the 20 MW threshold and recommends 50 MW, the level PJM used in its Critical Issue Fast Path proposal. A 50 MW load reliably triggers a new substation and material bulk-system impact, while a 20 MW load may not.
quotes: ODEC does not support the proposed 20 MW threshold for defining "large loads" and recommends that the Commission not follow the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Agreement and Procedures in this regard.
We believe a threshold of 50 MW is more appropriate and ensures that reforms focus on projects with a material impact on the bulk power system.

letters.desc: OMS argues the proposed 20 MW minimum is too low and would swamp the queue with smaller customers, defeating the efficiency goals of the ANOPR. Existing state large-load tariffs use thresholds of 100 to 150 MW, which OMS views as a more appropriate benchmark.
quotes: Defining large loads as any interconnecting customer demanding a minimum of 20 MW would likely limit any efficiencies or benefits intended by the ANOPR due to the sheer number of prospective large loads.
many other states have approved or are considering large load tariffs that all contemplate a range of 100-150 MW.

letters.desc: OPSI contends the proposed 20 MW applicability threshold is too low to produce meaningful efficiency gains and would conflict with PJM-region states that have set thresholds ranging from 25 to 100 MW.
quotes: the reforms in this docket should apply to new loads greater than 20 MW. This threshold is likely too small to make interconnection processes meaningfully more efficient and may overtake state-level proceedings where voltage thresholds have been set higher than this threshold. States in the PJM region are considering or have approved thresholds for large load additions ranging from 25 to 100 MW.

letters.desc: The PA PUC contends that a 20 MW individual threshold without aggregate limits captures well-functioning industrial interconnections beyond data centers and conflicts with existing state-approved tariff thresholds. The breadth of the threshold amplifies the major-questions concern.
quotes: The ANOPR exacerbates the issue by targeting reforms to all new loads greater than 20 MW. Even more, the rulemaking does not address aggregate thresholds and probably captures commercial/industrial customers other than data centers.
The impact of capturing all smaller non-data-center facilities above the 20 MW threshold would have a seismic impact on industrial load interconnections that have been well-functioning for decades.

The proposed rules conflict with state-approved tariffs for large industrial load that already address large load industrial tariffs with individual and aggregate megawatt load thresholds different from the 20 MW (individual) proposed in this rulemaking.

letters.desc: PPL opposes the 20 MW threshold as too low, noting it would sweep in longstanding industrial and commercial loads on sub-100 kV lines. PPL recommends a threshold of 100 MW or 500 MW to limit federal reach to genuinely new bulk-system loads while still covering most data centers.
quotes: This relatively low threshold will ensure that FERC regulation reaches not just hyperscalers and other large data centers, but many longstanding industrial and commercial customers, including many connected at transmission voltages below 100 kV.

If the Commission is seeking a lighter touch that only impacts the new class of loads connecting to the bulk electric system, it could consider a higher threshold such as 100 MW, or even 500 MW (thresholds that would still catch many data centers).

letters.desc: RSI argues the 20 MW threshold is arbitrary because it simply copies the generation interconnection cutoff without justification for load. RSI proposes replacing it with a wholesale-market-participation criterion that applies regardless of MW size.
quotes: The proposed ANOPR's entire basis for selecting the 20 MW threshold is that 20 MW is the threshold for the Commission's large generation interconnection process (LGIP) and agreement (LGIA). DOE did not provide support for why the MW threshold for generation should also be applied to load.
comparison of large loads connecting at the transmission level to large generators connecting to transmission is incongruent.

delineating the applicability of a federalized agreement and process based on the interaction with wholesale markets keeps the Commission from having to make arbitrary determinations. As such, RSI's proposal would be available to any size load, as long as they meet the other criteria for its applicability

letters.desc: SPP opposes a single federal MW threshold and argues that what counts as "large" depends on the voltage level of interconnection and local system conditions. SPP's own tariff uses 10 MW at or below 69 kV and 50 MW above 69 kV. SPP wants final rules to let each transmission provider set its own thresholds.
quotes: SPP requests that any final rules in this matter do not include any specific MW threshold, but instead, the final rules should allow each transmission provider to propose thresholds specific to the needs of their transmission systems.

SPP proposed the following threshold to qualify as a HILL: "(1) 10 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a voltage level less than or equal to 69 kV; or (2) 50 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a voltage level greater than 69 kV."

letters.desc: The VSCC opposes any fixed MW threshold for a federally run large load queue, arguing it creates incentives for applicants to game the cutoff. A split queue also harms non-large-load customers by separating planning for different load classes.
quotes: Develop a set of Commission-mandated minimum standards for large load interconnections, such as study deposits, site control requirements, and similar criteria while allowing transmission owners, and not the RTOs, who already face long delays and inefficiencies in their existing generation queues, to continue to manage large load interconnection queues with direct oversight of their state regulatory commissions.

The alternative approach envisioned by the ANOPR, which would establish one queue at the RTO for "large loads" and a different queue at the local utility for every other end-use customer still left with the utility, would create planning and study inefficiencies and could potentially disrupt other important loads, like manufacturers and commercial load, from being able to interconnect in a timely manner.

An arbitrary MW-based threshold for a Commission-regulated large load queue could lead to gamesmanship where loads are incentivized to come just above or just below the MW threshold in order to qualify for a state-run or federally-run queue.

letters.desc: Vistra opposes the DOE ANOPR's proposed 20 MW threshold because it is not tied to any analysis of how a load actually affects the transmission system. The Commission should instead set the threshold at a level that corresponds to likely transmission use or impact.
quotes: FERC should not adopt the 20 MW threshold proposed in the DOE ANOPR Proposal.  The 20 MW threshold does not appear to be tied to any particular conclusion about the interaction between the large load and the transmission system.  Rather, the Commission should consider a MW threshold at a level that corresponds to likely use of or impact on the transmission system.

letters.org: Wisconsin Electric Power CompanyWisconsin Public Service Corporation
